chapters.title: Count Work Before Measuring Time
chapters.markdown:
# Count Work Before Measuring Time

Original dhimantAI companion lesson for **Zen of Assembly Language** by Michael Abrash.

## Reading assignment

Read the opening discussion of high-performance programming and measurement in the linked restoration. Its processor timings describe historical hardware.

- [Authorized electronic restoration](https://github.com/jagregory/abrash-zen-of-asm)

## The idea

A performance claim needs a workload, a correct baseline and a measurement boundary. Counting comparisons is a useful first model because you can check the count by hand. It does not establish elapsed time: cache behavior, interpreter overhead and data layout can change the result. Start with the operation that dominates the actual workload, then measure the entire operation the user experiences.

Consider checking whether each requested identifier occurs in a list. A linear scan can compare every request with every stored identifier. Constructing a set once may reduce repeated lookup work, but that construction is part of the cost. For one request it may not pay off. Preserve order and duplicate behavior when replacing an algorithm. A faster program that returns different answers is a different program.

## Predict before running

Move 5 to the first position. Which result stays unchanged, and which cost changes?

## Worked Python concept lab

This is an original Python illustration. The book's language and runtime may differ. Copy it to a Python notebook to run it; reading this page does not execute code.

```python
items = [8, 3, 5, 1]
requests = [5, 9]
comparisons = 0
found = []
for request in requests:
    match = False
    for item in items:
        comparisons += 1
        if item == request:
            match = True
            break
    found.append(match)
print(found)
print(comparisons)
```

Expected output:

```text
[True, False]
7
```

The successful request compares 8, 3 and 5: three comparisons. The missing request scans all four values. Total: seven. The count says nothing yet about nanoseconds.

## Try it

Implement a set-based version. Test repeated requests, an empty list and missing identifiers. Record set construction separately from lookup when timing, then include both in an end-to-end measurement.

## Transfer task

Choose a real repeated lookup in a small program. State the workload, compare outputs first, collect repeated timings, and explain a case where the baseline is preferable.

Write your reasoning and tests in your own notebook. Record any help used. These activities and Study quizzes are practice; reading or receiving help does not establish independent mastery.

chapters.title: Preserve the Machine Contract
chapters.markdown:
# Preserve the Machine Contract

Original dhimantAI companion lesson for **Zen of Assembly Language** by Michael Abrash.

## Reading assignment

Read an assembly example involving registers or arithmetic. Identify register width and flag assumptions before comparing it to a high-level version.

- [Authorized electronic restoration](https://github.com/jagregory/abrash-zen-of-asm)

## The idea

A mathematical integer has no fixed width. An unsigned machine value does. Reducing an integer modulo 2 to the power w models wrapping to w bits, but it does not model every processor flag or language rule. Signed overflow, shifts and division require their own contracts. Python integers grow, whereas the modeled byte below wraps at 256.

Before optimizing a low-level operation, write down input range, representation and required outputs. Include boundary cases at zero, the largest representable value and the wrap boundary. Replacing arithmetic with a bit operation can preserve a value under one contract and break it under another. Do not transfer an old processor's speed recommendation to today's hardware without a new measurement.

## Predict before running

For byte inputs 127 and 1, is there unsigned carry? Would the signed interpretation tell the same story?

## Worked Python concept lab

This is an original Python illustration. The book's language and runtime may differ. Copy it to a Python notebook to run it; reading this page does not execute code.

```python
def byte_add(a, b):
    total = a + b
    return total & 255, total > 255

for pair in [(12, 20), (250, 10), (255, 1)]:
    print(byte_add(*pair))
```

Expected output:

```text
(32, False)
(4, True)
(0, True)
```

260 modulo 256 is 4. The separate Boolean records carry out for two unsigned byte inputs. It is not the signed-overflow flag.

## Try it

Add input validation for integers in 0..255. Write tests distinguishing unsigned carry from the signed interpretation of 127 + 1. Explain why this function is not a complete CPU emulator.

## Transfer task

Review a proposed bit-level optimization. Supply the exact input domain and either an equivalence argument or a counterexample.

Write your reasoning and tests in your own notebook. Record any help used. These activities and Study quizzes are practice; reading or receiving help does not establish independent mastery.

chapters.title: Optimize the Part That Matters
chapters.markdown:
# Optimize the Part That Matters

Original dhimantAI companion lesson for **Zen of Assembly Language** by Michael Abrash.

## Reading assignment

Return to the book’s measurement examples. Separate local instruction savings from whole-program improvement.

- [Authorized electronic restoration](https://github.com/jagregory/abrash-zen-of-asm)

## The idea

A local speedup is limited by the fraction of total work it affects. If a program spends 60 milliseconds in one operation and 40 elsewhere, making the first operation three times faster gives 20 + 40 = 60 milliseconds. The whole program is only about 1.67 times faster. Even an infinitely fast first operation cannot remove the other 40 milliseconds.

Use this model to choose experiments, not to manufacture benchmarks. Real changes may move costs, allocate more memory or change cache behavior. Measure representative sizes and repeated runs; document machine, runtime and input. Compare correctness before interpreting timing. When a result is noisy, report the range and investigate rather than selecting the fastest observation.

## Predict before running

What is the whole-program speedup if the 60-millisecond part is merely twice as fast?

## Worked Python concept lab

This is an original Python illustration. The book's language and runtime may differ. Copy it to a Python notebook to run it; reading this page does not execute code.

```python
baseline = 100
improved_part = 60 / 3
unchanged = 40
new_total = improved_part + unchanged
print(f"new total: {new_total:.0f} ms")
print(f"speedup: {baseline / new_total:.2f}x")
print(f"limit: {baseline / unchanged:.2f}x")
```

Expected output:

```text
new total: 60 ms
speedup: 1.67x
limit: 2.50x
```

The model holds the remaining 40 milliseconds constant. Its 2.5x limit applies only under that assumption.

## Try it

Build a table for local speedups of 1, 2, 4 and 10. Explain diminishing returns without claiming the model is measured evidence.

## Transfer task

Write an optimization report containing equivalent outputs, a workload description, timing observations, uncertainty and the next bottleneck.

Write your reasoning and tests in your own notebook. Record any help used. These activities and Study quizzes are practice; reading or receiving help does not establish independent mastery.

chapters.title: Make Stack Effects Visible
chapters.markdown:
# Make Stack Effects Visible

Original dhimantAI companion lesson for **Scientific Forth** by Julian V. Noble.

## Reading assignment

Use a lawful copy of Scientific Forth for its Forth and scientific-computing discussion. The linked resource describes the book; it is not a full-text download.

- [Book and scientific-computing context](https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~jwavrik/Forth/resources.html)

## The idea

A stack-based operation consumes values from the top of a stack and leaves its results there. A stack-effect comment describes the contract, not the implementation. For subtraction, write ( a b -- a-b ): b is popped first but a remains the left operand. Swapping these roles is a common error that addition will conceal.

Compose small operations only after their stack effects agree. An operation requiring two values must reject underflow before mutating the stack. This makes failure easier to understand and preserves useful diagnostic state. The Python function below models one tiny operation. It is not an implementation of Forth, whose words, dictionary and execution model require separate study.

## Predict before running

What happens to [99, 5, 12]? What should happen to [99]?

## Worked Python concept lab

This is an original Python illustration. The book's language and runtime may differ. Copy it to a Python notebook to run it; reading this page does not execute code.

```python
def subtract(stack):
    if len(stack) < 2:
        raise ValueError("two operands required")
    b = stack.pop()
    a = stack.pop()
    stack.append(a - b)

values = [99, 12, 5]
subtract(values)
print(values)
```

Expected output:

```text
[99, 7]
```

Only the last two items are consumed. The unrelated 99 remains beneath the result. Operand order is observable because subtraction is not commutative.

## Try it

Implement a division operation with an explicit policy for division by zero. Validate before removing either operand. Test that failure leaves the original stack intact.

## Transfer task

Design and document stack effects for a small expression evaluator. Trace a noncommutative expression and show one invalid expression it rejects.

Write your reasoning and tests in your own notebook. Record any help used. These activities and Study quizzes are practice; reading or receiving help does not establish independent mastery.

chapters.title: Approximation Needs an Error Argument
chapters.markdown:
# Approximation Needs an Error Argument

Original dhimantAI companion lesson for **Scientific Forth** by Julian V. Noble.

## Reading assignment

Read the book’s numerical integration material, comparing its assumptions and stopping rules with your own calculation.

- [Book and scientific-computing context](https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~jwavrik/Forth/resources.html)

## The idea

A numerical estimate is a claim about an approximation, not merely a printed number. The trapezoidal rule replaces a curve on each subinterval with a straight segment. Its endpoint values receive half weight while interior values receive full weight. Refining the grid often improves the estimate for a smooth function, but agreement between two grids alone is not a proof of accuracy.

Use a function with a known integral while developing the method. For f(x)=x² on [0,1], the exact integral is 1/3. This gives an independent error check. Keep discretization error separate from floating-point rounding. Functions with sharp peaks or discontinuities can need different grids and analysis. A stopping criterion must include a finite iteration budget and a clear result when the requested tolerance is not reached.

## Predict before running

Why is the estimate above the exact integral for this convex curve?

## Worked Python concept lab

This is an original Python illustration. The book's language and runtime may differ. Copy it to a Python notebook to run it; reading this page does not execute code.

```python
def trapezoid(n):
    h = 1 / n
    total = 0.5 * (0**2 + 1**2)
    for i in range(1, n):
        total += (i * h)**2
    return h * total

for n in (2, 4):
    estimate = trapezoid(n)
    print(n, f"{estimate:.6f}", f"error={estimate - 1/3:.6f}")
```

Expected output:

```text
2 0.375000 error=0.041667
4 0.343750 error=0.010417
```

Doubling n reduces the error by a factor of four for this quadratic example. That observed ratio is not a guarantee for arbitrary functions.

## Try it

Generalize to f, a, b and positive n. Test a constant function, a linear function and x². Reject n=0 before dividing.

## Transfer task

Compare two numerical methods on a function with a known answer. Report approximation error, evaluation count and the conditions under which your comparison is meaningful.

Write your reasoning and tests in your own notebook. Record any help used. These activities and Study quizzes are practice; reading or receiving help does not establish independent mastery.

chapters.title: Data Layout Is Part of the Algorithm
chapters.markdown:
# Data Layout Is Part of the Algorithm

Original dhimantAI companion lesson for **Scientific Forth** by Julian V. Noble.

## Reading assignment

Read a matrix-computation example and identify its dimension and storage conventions.

- [Book and scientific-computing context](https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~jwavrik/Forth/resources.html)

## The idea

A matrix operation has both a mathematical shape and a physical representation. For row-major storage with c columns, position (r,k) is stored at r*c+k. A matrix-vector product requires the vector length to equal the number of columns; the output length equals the number of rows. An example with a square matrix alone can hide a transposition bug.

Write a rectangular example whose rows have visibly different results. Check dimensions before computation, including ragged rows. Distinguish a layout change from a mathematical transpose. Optimizing memory access should preserve the mapping from coordinates to values. In numerical work also ask whether reordering a sum changes rounding enough to matter for the application.

## Predict before running

Which entries would a mistaken column-major interpretation use for the first output?

## Worked Python concept lab

This is an original Python illustration. The book's language and runtime may differ. Copy it to a Python notebook to run it; reading this page does not execute code.

```python
rows, cols = 2, 3
flat = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
vector = [2, 0, -1]
result = [sum(flat[r * cols + c] * vector[c] for c in range(cols))
          for r in range(rows)]
print(result)
```

Expected output:

```text
[-1, 2]
```

The first row gives 1*2 + 2*0 - 3 = -1. The second gives 4*2 + 5*0 - 6 = 2. The two outputs expose the row boundary.

## Try it

Write a checked matrix-vector function. Test a 1×3 matrix, a 3×1 matrix, a zero vector and incompatible dimensions. Document the empty-matrix policy.

## Transfer task

Implement the same operation with two storage layouts and verify equivalent results on rectangular inputs before measuring either version.

Write your reasoning and tests in your own notebook. Record any help used. These activities and Study quizzes are practice; reading or receiving help does not establish independent mastery.

chapters.title: Treat Shapes as Data
chapters.markdown:
# Treat Shapes as Data

Original dhimantAI companion lesson for **Fractals, Visualization, and J** by Clifford Reiter.

## Reading assignment

Read the author’s sample section 1.1 on J arithmetic and the table of contents. Compare array thinking with scalar loops.

- [Author’s book page and sample sections](https://webbox.lafayette.edu/~reiterc/j/fvj4/index.html)

## The idea

A point can be represented as a pair and a shape as a sequence of points. Applying the same transformation to every point separates the geometry from traversal. In an array language such as J, shape and rank influence how an operation applies; these are semantic facts, not cosmetic details. Our Python list traversal is a bridge to the idea, not a translation of J syntax.

A transformation needs a coordinate convention. Here x grows to the right and y grows upward. Screen coordinates often reverse y. Scaling and translation generally do not commute: translate then scale also scales the translation. Use an asymmetric shape so an accidental reflection or swapped coordinate is visible. Preserve numeric coordinates as evidence alongside the drawing.

## Predict before running

Which translation would make move-then-scale equal scale-then-move?

## Worked Python concept lab

This is an original Python illustration. The book's language and runtime may differ. Copy it to a Python notebook to run it; reading this page does not execute code.

```python
points = [(0, 0), (2, 0), (0, 1)]
scale_then_move = [(2*x + 3, 2*y - 1) for x, y in points]
move_then_scale = [(2*(x + 3), 2*(y - 1)) for x, y in points]
print(scale_then_move)
print(move_then_scale)
```

Expected output:

```text
[(3, -1), (7, -1), (3, 1)]
[(6, -2), (10, -2), (6, 0)]
```

Both triangles double their side lengths, but the translations differ. Matching shape alone would miss the error.

## Try it

Implement a 90-degree rotation (x,y)→(-y,x). Verify four rotations restore every original point, including negative coordinates.

## Transfer task

Create a small transformation pipeline and a coordinate table. Explain its order, coordinate convention and two invariants before drawing it.

Write your reasoning and tests in your own notebook. Record any help used. These activities and Study quizzes are practice; reading or receiving help does not establish independent mastery.

chapters.title: Iteration Creates Structure
chapters.markdown:
# Iteration Creates Structure

Original dhimantAI companion lesson for **Fractals, Visualization, and J** by Clifford Reiter.

## Reading assignment

Read the sample on collages of transformations and the material on iterated function systems.

- [Author’s book page and sample sections](https://webbox.lafayette.edu/~reiterc/j/fvj4/index.html)

## The idea

Repeated simple transformations can produce complex structure. Keep the transformation rule separate from the iteration policy. A deterministic construction applies a fixed set of maps at each round; a random iteration samples maps. They have different output counts and reproducibility requirements. Recording the seed helps reproduce a random experiment but does not prove it has sampled the limiting set adequately.

The example builds endpoints of two contracted copies of an interval. Each round multiplies the number of listed points by two. After a finite number of rounds you have a finite approximation, not an infinite fractal. To reason about resolution, track contraction factor and iteration depth together. Avoid claiming a fractal dimension merely because the picture looks self-similar.

## Predict before running

How many listed points appear after five rounds from these two starting points?

## Worked Python concept lab

This is an original Python illustration. The book's language and runtime may differ. Copy it to a Python notebook to run it; reading this page does not execute code.

```python
points = [0.0, 1.0]
for _ in range(2):
    points = [y for x in points for y in (x/3, (x+2)/3)]
print(len(points))
print([round(x, 3) for x in sorted(points)])
```

Expected output:

```text
8
[0.0, 0.111, 0.222, 0.333, 0.667, 0.778, 0.889, 1.0]
```

Two maps are applied to each input point in each round. The gap between one third and two thirds remains empty.

## Try it

Generate three further rounds with a fixed maximum depth. Check every point remains in [0,1] and explain why that bound follows from both maps.

## Transfer task

Explore a two-dimensional contraction system. Record rules, initial state and depth; distinguish properties you proved from patterns you only observed.

Write your reasoning and tests in your own notebook. Record any help used. These activities and Study quizzes are practice; reading or receiving help does not establish independent mastery.

chapters.title: Make the Picture Tell the Truth
chapters.markdown:
# Make the Picture Tell the Truth

Original dhimantAI companion lesson for **Fractals, Visualization, and J** by Clifford Reiter.

## Reading assignment

Read the author’s color-space sample and compare its choices with a visualization you construct.

- [Author’s book page and sample sections](https://webbox.lafayette.edu/~reiterc/j/fvj4/index.html)

## The idea

A visualization is a chain from data to coordinates to color. Errors in any mapping can create a persuasive but false picture. For an escape-time experiment, store the number of iterations separately from its color. A point that has not escaped after a finite budget is unresolved by that computation; it is not thereby proved to belong to the infinite set.

When comparing images, keep viewport, resolution, iteration budget and color scale explicit. Autoscaling each image independently can make unequal magnitudes look identical. A legend is part of the result. Inspect a few known points numerically before trusting the image. Separate computational evidence from aesthetic choices such as palette and smoothing.

## Predict before running

What changes if the implementation incorrectly uses >= 2?

## Worked Python concept lab

This is an original Python illustration. The book's language and runtime may differ. Copy it to a Python notebook to run it; reading this page does not execute code.

```python
def escape(c, budget=10):
    z = 0j
    for step in range(1, budget + 1):
        z = z*z + c
        if abs(z) > 2:
            return step
    return None

for c in (0j, 1+0j, 2+0j):
    print(c, escape(c))
```

Expected output:

```text
0j None
(1+0j) 3
(2+0j) 2
```

For c=1 the magnitudes are 1, 2 and 5; escape occurs on step three because the comparison is strictly greater than two. None means no escape within ten iterations.

## Try it

Make a small coordinate grid and export its escape counts before choosing colors. Include a separate color for unresolved points and a legend for counts.

## Transfer task

Compare two iteration budgets with the same viewport and color scale. Identify which conclusions are supported and which need further computation or proof.

Write your reasoning and tests in your own notebook. Record any help used. These activities and Study quizzes are practice; reading or receiving help does not establish independent mastery.

chapters.title: Read an Interview as a Design Case
chapters.markdown:
# Read an Interview as a Design Case

Original dhimantAI companion lesson for **Programmers at Work** by Susan Lammers.

## Reading assignment

Choose an excerpt on the author’s site. Record the speaker, source link and constraints explicitly mentioned; do not invent missing details.

- [Author’s interviews and book information](https://www.programmersatwork.net/)

## The idea

An interview reports a person's experience. It is evidence about that account, not a controlled comparison proving a universal method. Separate what the speaker states from your inference. Ask what constraints shaped the decision: memory, hardware, deadlines, users or team size. A strategy can be sensible under one constraint and costly under another.

Turn one account into a decision record: problem, constraints, alternatives, choice and evidence that would change the choice. A numerical budget makes assumptions visible. The invented example below is a classroom scenario, not a claim about anyone in the book. It compares a dense grid and a compact representation under a fixed memory budget. Metadata and alignment are excluded explicitly.

## Predict before running

Which unmodeled costs could reverse the choice for a different workload?

## Worked Python concept lab

This is an original Python illustration. The book's language and runtime may differ. Copy it to a Python notebook to run it; reading this page does not execute code.

```python
budget = 64 * 1024
cells = 80 * 25
dense_bytes = cells * 4
compact_bytes = cells * 2
print(dense_bytes, compact_bytes)
print(budget - dense_bytes, budget - compact_bytes)
```

Expected output:

```text
8000 4000
57536 61536
```

The compact representation saves 4,000 bytes in this simplified model. It may require extra decoding work, so the memory comparison alone cannot select the design.

## Try it

Write a decision record for a synthetic 64 KiB tool. Compare two representations, state excluded costs, and define a measurement needed before committing.

## Transfer task

Analyze one linked interview excerpt. Label direct observations and your interpretations separately, then explain how a changed constraint could justify a different design.

Write your reasoning and tests in your own notebook. Record any help used. These activities and Study quizzes are practice; reading or receiving help does not establish independent mastery.

chapters.title: Prototype the Risky Assumption
chapters.markdown:
# Prototype the Risky Assumption

Original dhimantAI companion lesson for **Programmers at Work** by Susan Lammers.

## Reading assignment

Read an excerpt describing how a programmer developed an idea. Identify what evidence the account actually provides about prototypes or feedback.

- [Author’s interviews and book information](https://www.programmersatwork.net/)

## The idea

A prototype is useful when it answers a decision, such as whether an interaction can fit a latency budget. Building many features before identifying that decision can produce a polished demonstration without reducing the main uncertainty. Define the assumption, observable outcome, smallest experiment and threshold before collecting results.

Synthetic data tests your analysis code; it does not establish real user behavior. The observations below are invented response times in milliseconds. Their maximum violates a hypothetical 200 ms threshold even though their average looks acceptable. Choose a statistic that matches the user requirement, and state the sampling limits. Do not silently redefine the target after seeing the results.

## Predict before running

Would a mean-only acceptance rule detect the slow observation?

## Worked Python concept lab

This is an original Python illustration. The book's language and runtime may differ. Copy it to a Python notebook to run it; reading this page does not execute code.

```python
times_ms = [80, 95, 110, 420, 90]
print(f"mean={sum(times_ms)/len(times_ms):.0f} ms")
print(f"maximum={max(times_ms)} ms")
print(sum(t > 200 for t in times_ms), "over budget")
```

Expected output:

```text
mean=159 ms
maximum=420 ms
1 over budget
```

The mean is below 200 ms, but one of five observations is above it. Five invented observations cannot estimate a production tail reliably.

## Try it

Design an experiment for a command-search prototype. State the task, workload, latency statistic, budget and failure response. Keep synthetic checks separate from collected measurements.

## Transfer task

Build or sketch the smallest prototype that could falsify one design assumption. Report what remains unknown after the experiment.

Write your reasoning and tests in your own notebook. Record any help used. These activities and Study quizzes are practice; reading or receiving help does not establish independent mastery.

chapters.title: Explain Tradeoffs Without Hero Stories
chapters.markdown:
# Explain Tradeoffs Without Hero Stories

Original dhimantAI companion lesson for **Programmers at Work** by Susan Lammers.

## Reading assignment

Compare two excerpts from different programmers. Preserve their context rather than treating either as universal advice.

- [Author’s interviews and book information](https://www.programmersatwork.net/)

## The idea

A decision can be reviewed even when there is no single best answer. State the criteria and constraints, then compare alternatives under them. A weighted score makes priorities explicit but can also disguise arbitrary preferences as arithmetic. Keep the original measurements or judgments beside the aggregate score and perform a sensitivity check.

The example uses invented ratings where higher is better. It asks whether valuing simplicity or throughput changes the choice. These scores are not benchmarks. If a small weight change reverses the recommendation, the decision is sensitive and needs a clear product priority. A useful engineering handoff records that uncertainty so a later maintainer can reconsider it.

## Predict before running

What happens when the two criteria have equal weight?

## Worked Python concept lab

This is an original Python illustration. The book's language and runtime may differ. Copy it to a Python notebook to run it; reading this page does not execute code.

```python
ratings = {"simple": (5, 2), "fast": (2, 5)}
for simplicity_weight in (0.8, 0.2):
    scores = {name: simplicity_weight*s + (1-simplicity_weight)*t
              for name, (s, t) in ratings.items()}
    print(simplicity_weight, max(scores, key=scores.get))
```

Expected output:

```text
0.8 simple
0.2 fast
```

The alternatives swap rank when priorities change. The calculation exposes the preference; it does not validate the ratings.

## Try it

Write a short design review with two alternatives, a hard constraint, two softer criteria and one uncertainty. Identify what is measured and what is judgment.

## Transfer task

Create a one-page engineering case study from your own small project: context, decision, evidence, outcome and what you would change under a different constraint.

Write your reasoning and tests in your own notebook. Record any help used. These activities and Study quizzes are practice; reading or receiving help does not establish independent mastery.

chapters.title: Decompose by Responsibility
chapters.markdown:
# Decompose by Responsibility

Original dhimantAI companion lesson for **Thinking Forth** by Leo Brodie.

## Reading assignment

Read the book’s analysis and decomposition discussions. Follow its official download link for the original text.

- [Thinking Forth project and free reading edition](https://thinking-forth.sourceforge.net/)

## The idea

Decomposition begins with what the program must accomplish. Identify responsibilities that can be named and checked independently: reading input, validating it, computing a result and presenting it. Splitting every line into a function creates indirection without necessarily clarifying a responsibility. A useful boundary has a coherent purpose and an explicit contract.

The example separates a parcel's base charge from a rush surcharge. Its thresholds are business rules in an invented exercise. Name the unit and validate the allowed range. Think about which rule is likely to change and which caller should remain unaffected. Composition works best when each component's outputs satisfy the next component's input contract.

## Predict before running

Which boundary test catches an accidental < 500 condition?

## Worked Python concept lab

This is an original Python illustration. The book's language and runtime may differ. Copy it to a Python notebook to run it; reading this page does not execute code.

```python
def base_charge(grams):
    if grams <= 0:
        raise ValueError("positive grams required")
    return 40 if grams <= 500 else 70

def charge(grams, rush):
    return base_charge(grams) + (25 if rush else 0)

print(charge(500, False))
print(charge(501, True))
```

Expected output:

```text
40
95
```

500 grams stays in the first band. 501 grams uses the second band, then adds 25 for rush service. The function names separate the two reasons for change.

## Try it

Add a separate packaging charge with a documented rule. Keep base-charge tests unchanged and add tests for the composition.

## Transfer task

Decompose a small input-to-report program into responsibilities. Explain each boundary using its contract, not its line count.

Write your reasoning and tests in your own notebook. Record any help used. These activities and Study quizzes are practice; reading or receiving help does not establish independent mastery.

chapters.title: Choose Names That Preserve Meaning
chapters.markdown:
# Choose Names That Preserve Meaning

Original dhimantAI companion lesson for **Thinking Forth** by Leo Brodie.

## Reading assignment

Read the book’s naming, style and convention material. Notice how a small vocabulary communicates the problem domain.

- [Thinking Forth project and free reading edition](https://thinking-forth.sourceforge.net/)

## The idea

Names should tell a reader what is represented and what an operation promises. A bare number called amount can mean currency, minor currency units or a quantity. A domain word with a documented invariant reduces repeated interpretation. Forth's vocabulary of small words highlights this idea, but the principle applies across languages.

Representation choices must be visible at boundaries. Store money in integer minor units when the domain permits it, and define rounding explicitly when a computation creates fractions. The example never uses floating-point money. It accepts prices in cents and returns cents. That does not solve tax policy or currency conversion; those are separate contracts requiring separate rules.

## Predict before running

Why would naming the result subtotal without its unit make later code harder to review?

## Worked Python concept lab

This is an original Python illustration. The book's language and runtime may differ. Copy it to a Python notebook to run it; reading this page does not execute code.

```python
def line_total_cents(unit_price_cents, quantity):
    if unit_price_cents < 0 or quantity < 0:
        raise ValueError("nonnegative values required")
    return unit_price_cents * quantity

subtotal_cents = line_total_cents(125, 3)
print(subtotal_cents)
print(f"{subtotal_cents // 100}.{subtotal_cents % 100:02d}")
```

Expected output:

```text
375
3.75
```

The calculation yields 375 cents. Formatting splits whole units from the remainder; it does not change the stored amount.

## Try it

Add a basket total from line items. Keep formatting out of the arithmetic functions. Test an empty basket and a zero quantity.

## Transfer task

Review a function with ambiguous names. Propose a small domain vocabulary, document units and invariants, and show a test that catches a unit mismatch.

chapters.title: Factor Without Changing Behavior
chapters.markdown:
# Factor Without Changing Behavior

Original dhimantAI companion lesson for **Thinking Forth** by Leo Brodie.

## Reading assignment

Read the book’s factoring discussion. Compare reducing duplication with choosing the right abstraction boundary.

- [Thinking Forth project and free reading edition](https://thinking-forth.sourceforge.net/)

## The idea

A refactoring preserves externally observable behavior under an explicit contract. Begin with examples that capture current rules, especially awkward boundaries. Removing duplication is useful when the repeated code expresses the same rule. Two similar fragments may represent different policies that will change independently; merging them prematurely can hide that distinction.

Use an independent oracle or a small exhaustive domain to compare versions. Testing every value in a finite range proves equality on that range, not for every possible input. The example extracts one predicate from a fee rule. It retains precedence: a waived fee wins before membership is considered. Recording that precedence is more valuable than merely shortening the function.

## Predict before running

Which ages are most important if you cannot enumerate the entire domain?

## Worked Python concept lab

This is an original Python illustration. The book's language and runtime may differ. Copy it to a Python notebook to run it; reading this page does not execute code.

```python
def old_fee(age, member):
    if age < 6 or age >= 65:
        return 0
    if member:
        return 8
    return 12

def waived(age):
    return age < 6 or age >= 65

def new_fee(age, member):
    return 0 if waived(age) else (8 if member else 12)

print(all(old_fee(a, m) == new_fee(a, m)
          for a in range(121) for m in (False, True)))
```

Expected output:

```text
True
```

The comparison covers 242 input pairs: ages 0 through 120 with both membership values. Negative ages are outside the stated checked domain.

## Try it

Introduce a deliberate boundary bug and show that the comparison catches it. Then add explicit domain validation to both versions before comparing again.

## Transfer task

Refactor a small program with a written behavior contract, boundary tests and an explanation of why each extracted function represents one stable responsibility.

chapters.markdown:
# Abstract a Pattern of Computation

Original dhimantAI companion lesson for **Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs** by Harold Abelson and Gerald Jay Sussman, with Julie Sussman.

## Reading assignment

Read SICP sections 1.2 and 1.3 on processes and higher-order procedures. Compare the Scheme notation with the Python bridge below.

- [MIT Press book and open-access edition](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262510875/structure-and-interpretation-of-computer-programs/)
- [Scheme and JavaScript comparison edition](https://sicp.sourceacademy.org/)

## The idea

An abstraction separates the part that stays the same from the part that varies. A fold visits a sequence while updating an accumulator. Its combination function and initial value determine the result. Choosing zero for a sum works because zero is the additive identity; choosing zero for a product would erase all nonempty products.

Reason about the process as well as its final value. A recursive definition can create deferred operations or update state as it proceeds. Python does not provide Scheme-style proper tail calls, so translating a tail-recursive Scheme process directly may change its space behavior. The loop below makes the accumulator explicit and avoids accumulating recursive call frames. Memory use still depends on the accumulator and combiner: the numeric examples keep one running number, while collecting partial results in a growing list requires growing storage.

## Predict before running

Does replacing addition with subtraction make the fold order observable?

## Worked Python concept lab

This is an original Python illustration. The book's language and runtime may differ. Copy it to a Python notebook to run it; reading this page does not execute code.

```python
def fold(combine, initial, values):
    result = initial
    for value in values:
        result = combine(result, value)
    return result

print(fold(lambda a, b: a+b, 0, [2, 4, 6]))
print(fold(lambda a, b: a*b, 1, [2, 4, 6]))
print(fold(lambda a, b: a+b, 0, []))
```

Expected output:

```text
12
48
0
```

The traversal stays unchanged while combination and identity change. An empty input returns the chosen initial value.

## Try it

Trace subtraction with an initial value of 10 and inputs [1,2,3]. Compare a left fold with a right-associated expression. State the algebraic property needed to reassociate safely.

## Transfer task

Extract a higher-order operation from two small programs. Demonstrate the shared process, the varying parameter and an empty-input contract.

Write your reasoning and tests in your own notebook. Record any help used. These activities and Study quizzes are practice; reading or receiving help does not establish independent mastery.

chapters.title: Protect an Abstraction Barrier
chapters.markdown:
# Protect an Abstraction Barrier

Original dhimantAI companion lesson for **Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs** by Harold Abelson and Gerald Jay Sussman, with Julie Sussman.

## Reading assignment

Read sections 2.1 and 2.2 on data abstraction and compound data.

- [MIT Press book and open-access edition](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262510875/structure-and-interpretation-of-computer-programs/)
- [Scheme and JavaScript comparison edition](https://sicp.sourceacademy.org/)

## The idea

A data abstraction is defined by operations and laws, not by one storage format. Callers using constructors and selectors can remain unchanged when the representation changes. If callers inspect tuple positions or dictionary keys directly, they cross the abstraction barrier and couple themselves to the representation.

A rational-number constructor can normalize the sign and divide numerator and denominator by their greatest common divisor. Then equivalent values have the same representation. Denominator zero is invalid. This invariant simplifies equality, but arithmetic operations still need to honor it. Python integers avoid fixed-width overflow here; another language may need an overflow policy as part of the contract.

## Predict before running

What representation should rational(-6,-8) produce?

## Worked Python concept lab

This is an original Python illustration. The book's language and runtime may differ. Copy it to a Python notebook to run it; reading this page does not execute code.

```python
from math import gcd

def rational(n, d):
    if d == 0:
        raise ValueError("zero denominator")
    if d < 0:
        n, d = -n, -d
    common = gcd(n, d)
    return (n // common, d // common)

print(rational(6, -8))
print(rational(0, 9))
print(rational(3, 4) == rational(6, 8))
```

Expected output:

```text
(-3, 4)
(0, 1)
True
```

Sign normalization makes the denominator positive. gcd(0,9)=9 gives the canonical zero representation (0,1).

## Try it

Implement addition using constructors and selectors, then change storage from tuple to a small class. Keep caller tests unchanged.

## Transfer task

Design an abstraction for an interval or vector. State its laws, provide two representations and demonstrate that clients do not depend on either layout.

Write your reasoning and tests in your own notebook. Record any help used. These activities and Study quizzes are practice; reading or receiving help does not establish independent mastery.

# Make Evaluation Rules Explicit

Original dhimantAI companion lesson for **Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs** by Harold Abelson and Gerald Jay Sussman, with Julie Sussman.

## Reading assignment

Read chapter 4’s introduction to evaluators. This small expression-tree lab does not cover the full Scheme evaluator, environments or compiler.

- [MIT Press book and open-access edition](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262510875/structure-and-interpretation-of-computer-programs/)
- [Scheme and JavaScript comparison edition](https://sicp.sourceacademy.org/)

## The idea

An evaluator gives meaning to a representation of a program. Keep syntax, environment lookup and execution rules separate. The tiny language below contains integer literals and binary addition or multiplication nodes. Its evaluator recursively evaluates operands before applying the operator. It deliberately does not call Python eval.

A real language requires more: variables, environments, binding, procedures and error rules. Adding state also changes what can be substituted without changing behavior. Write down the small language's grammar before extending it. Reject malformed nodes rather than guessing their meaning. A test suite should include both valid programs and invalid syntax, because error behavior is part of the language contract.

## Predict before running

Which tree produces 2 + 3*4 instead, and what result should it give?

## Worked Python concept lab

This is an original Python illustration. The book's language and runtime may differ. Copy it to a Python notebook to run it; reading this page does not execute code.

```python
def evaluate(expr):
    if type(expr) is int:
        return expr
    if not isinstance(expr, tuple) or len(expr) != 3:
        raise ValueError("invalid expression")
    op, left, right = expr
    if op not in ("+", "*"):
        raise ValueError("unknown operator")
    a, b = evaluate(left), evaluate(right)
    return a+b if op == "+" else a*b

print(evaluate(("*", ("+", 2, 3), 4)))
```

Expected output:

```text
20
```

The inner addition yields 5, then multiplication yields 20. Tree shape carries grouping; no textual precedence rule is needed for this representation.

## Try it

Add variable lookup through an explicit environment dictionary. Reject missing names and unsupported node forms. Explain why this still is not a Scheme interpreter.

## Transfer task

Specify and implement a small expression language with tests for grouping, lookup and invalid syntax. Describe one feature that would require a richer environment model.

Write your reasoning and tests in your own notebook. Record any help used. These activities and Study quizzes are practice; reading or receiving help does not establish independent mastery.

chapters.title: Separate Patterns from Bindings
chapters.markdown:
# Separate Patterns from Bindings

Original dhimantAI companion lesson for **Paradigms of Artificial Intelligence Programming** by Peter Norvig.

## Reading assignment

Read the author’s chapters on Eliza and software tools, especially the pattern-matching discussion. Consult the Common Lisp code alongside the text.

- [Author’s book, chapters and Common Lisp code](https://github.com/norvig/paip-lisp)

## The idea

A symbolic matcher compares a pattern with input while accumulating variable bindings. Repeated occurrences of one variable must agree. A match that simply overwrites an earlier binding would accept contradictory inputs. A failed match should not leak partial bindings into a later attempt.

The example matches fixed-length token lists. Tokens beginning with ? are variables, and each variable matches exactly one token. This is far smaller than the book's pattern language: there are no segment variables, alternatives or unification of nested terms. State these limits so a simple matcher is not mistaken for a general understanding system. Matching a sentence pattern also does not establish that the sentence is true.

## Predict before running

How should an empty pattern behave with empty input? Why is an empty binding dictionary different from failure?

## Worked Python concept lab

This is an original Python illustration. The book's language and runtime may differ. Copy it to a Python notebook to run it; reading this page does not execute code.

```python
def match(pattern, tokens):
    if len(pattern) != len(tokens):
        return None
    bindings = {}
    for p, token in zip(pattern, tokens):
        if p.startswith("?"):
            if p in bindings and bindings[p] != token:
                return None
            bindings[p] = token
        elif p != token:
            return None
    return bindings

print(match(["?x", "likes", "?x"], ["Ada", "likes", "Ada"]))
print(match(["?x", "likes", "?x"], ["Ada", "likes", "Lin"]))
```

Expected output:

```text
{'?x': 'Ada'}
None
```

The first occurrence binds ?x to Ada. The second occurrence checks that same value rather than overwriting it.

## Try it

Add tests for literals, length mismatch, repeated variables and empty input. Keep each match independent. Explain why callers must test result is None rather than treating every empty dictionary as failure.

## Transfer task

Design a small command matcher with documented syntax and failure behavior. Include a counterexample to a matcher that overwrites repeated bindings.

Write your reasoning and tests in your own notebook. Record any help used. These activities and Study quizzes are practice; reading or receiving help does not establish independent mastery.

chapters.title: Search a State Space Deliberately
chapters.markdown:
# Search a State Space Deliberately

Original dhimantAI companion lesson for **Paradigms of Artificial Intelligence Programming** by Peter Norvig.

## Reading assignment

Read the general problem solver and search-tools chapters. Identify states, actions and goal tests separately.

- [Author’s book, chapters and Common Lisp code](https://github.com/norvig/paip-lisp)

## The idea

A search problem consists of states, transitions and a goal test. The search strategy determines which frontier item is explored next. Breadth-first search finds a path with the fewest edges when every edge has equal cost. It does not necessarily minimize travel time or another weighted cost. A visited set prevents repeated exploration of states in a finite graph.

Mark a state when it enters the frontier, not only when removed, to avoid unnecessary duplicate queue entries. Keep the chosen path or parent relation so the result can be inspected. For large or implicit spaces, add limits and distinguish exhausted search from a proven unreachable goal. The small graph below is finite and fully known.

## Predict before running

What happens to the selected path if A lists C before B?

## Worked Python concept lab

This is an original Python illustration. The book's language and runtime may differ. Copy it to a Python notebook to run it; reading this page does not execute code.

```python
from collections import deque

graph = {"A": ["B", "C"], "B": ["D"], "C": ["D"], "D": []}
queue = deque([("A", ["A"])])
seen = {"A"}
while queue:
    node, path = queue.popleft()
    if node == "D":
        print(path)
        break
    for neighbor in graph[node]:
        if neighbor not in seen:
            seen.add(neighbor)
            queue.append((neighbor, path + [neighbor]))
```

Expected output:

```text
['A', 'B', 'D']
```

B is enqueued before C, so this implementation chooses the path through B when shortest paths tie. Both alternatives have two edges.

## Try it

Extract a function returning a path or None. Test start=goal, a cycle and an unreachable node. State the deterministic tie-breaking rule.

## Transfer task

Model a small planning problem as states and transitions. Explain why your search strategy matches its cost model and how you report a search limit.

Write your reasoning and tests in your own notebook. Record any help used. These activities and Study quizzes are practice; reading or receiving help does not establish independent mastery.

chapters.title: Track What a Rule Engine Can Establish
chapters.markdown:
# Track What a Rule Engine Can Establish

Original dhimantAI companion lesson for **Paradigms of Artificial Intelligence Programming** by Peter Norvig.

## Reading assignment

Read the knowledge-representation or expert-system chapters. Distinguish symbolic inference from empirical confidence and from modern language-model output.

- [Author’s book, chapters and Common Lisp code](https://github.com/norvig/paip-lisp)

## The idea

A forward-chaining rule adds a conclusion when its premises are already known. In a finite monotonic system with no retractions, repeated application reaches a fixed point because facts only accumulate. Store the derivation for each inferred fact so a user can inspect why it appeared. A rule engine's conclusion is conditional on its premises and rules; it does not independently verify them.

The invented parcel example below is deliberately nonmedical. Its rules say nothing about facts outside this toy system. If a premise is missing, absence of a derivation is not proof of the opposite. Retractions, conflicting facts and uncertainty require additional semantics. Do not assign numerical confidence merely because several rules reach the same conclusion.

## Predict before running

Which new fact would allow dispatch, and which derivation would then explain it?

## Worked Python concept lab

This is an original Python illustration. The book's language and runtime may differ. Copy it to a Python notebook to run it; reading this page does not execute code.

```python
facts = {"paid", "packed"}
rules = [({"paid", "packed"}, "ready"), ({"ready", "labelled"}, "dispatch")]
reasons = {}
changed = True
while changed:
    changed = False
    for premises, conclusion in rules:
        if premises <= facts and conclusion not in facts:
            facts.add(conclusion)
            reasons[conclusion] = sorted(premises)
            changed = True
print(sorted(facts))
print(reasons)
```

Expected output:

```text
['packed', 'paid', 'ready']
{'ready': ['packed', 'paid']}
```

ready is inferred from paid and packed. dispatch is not inferred because labelled is absent. The engine has not proved that dispatch is impossible.

## Try it

Extract a fixed-point function and return both facts and reasons. Test a rule cycle, no applicable rules and multiple ways to derive one fact. Define how you choose a reason.

## Transfer task

Build a small, nonmedical rule-based assistant with transparent premises and derivations. Document how missing evidence differs from falsehood and where a human decision remains necessary.

Write your reasoning and tests in your own notebook. Record any help used. These activities and Study quizzes are practice; reading or receiving help does not establish independent mastery.
